findings.title: Uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls prisma.credential.update, but this file never imports prisma (imports are jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, HttpError, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). Any construction of SalesforceCalendarService will fail type-checking/compilation or throw ReferenceError at runtime when this line executes, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

findings.title: Stores SafeParse wrapper object as the credential key
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full zod SafeParse result ({success, data}), not the parsed data. This line assigns that result to `key` and persists it via prisma.credential.update({data:{key}}), whereas previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the credential object itself. The stored key becomes {success:true,data:{...}}, so the next googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) in googleAuth will fail and Google Calendar credentials become unusable after the first refresh, even when credential sharing is disabled.

findings.title: Minimum token schema strips expiry and provider-specific fields
findings.body: minimumTokenResponseSchema only declares access_token plus computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()], which are literal object-string keys, not wildcards. Zod strips unknown keys by default, so when sharing is enabled expires_in/expiry_date, scope, token_type, instance_url and other fields required by callers are dropped from .data. Zoom then computes expiry_date as Date.now()+undefined*1000 (NaN), Office365 keeps a stale expiry, and Salesforce loses id/instance_url/signature, producing invalid or immediately-expired credentials.

findings.title: Dummy refresh_token overwrites the real refresh token
findings.body: When the (stripped) parsed response has no refresh_token, this sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token". Callers persist that value: Zoom assigns key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token and Office365 spreads tokenResponse.data into the stored credential. With credential sharing enabled the real refresh token in the database is irreversibly replaced by the placeholder, so disabling sharing later or falling back to the provider leaves the credential permanently unrefreshable.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response incompatible with most callers
findings.body: When sharing is enabled this returns the raw fetch Response, but callers expect the shape of their original refreshFunction. Google expects res.data.access_token/expiry_date, HubSpot expects a HubspotToken object with expiresIn/accessToken, and Zoho CRM/Bigin expect an axios response with .data.error/access_token. A fetch Response has none of those properties, so those integrations store undefined tokens/expiry or throw on .data access instead of using the synced access token. Only fetch-based callers that parse JSON themselves are compatible.

findings.title: Passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId) sends its third argument to the sync endpoint as calcomUserId. Here credentialId (the credential row id, captured in biginAuth) is passed instead of credential.userId, which this method does not even receive. The parent platform will look up a user by a credential id, so it will return tokens for the wrong user or no user, and the refreshed token can be stored against this credential.

findings.title: Refreshed Salesforce token is discarded and stale token is used
findings.body: getClient unconditionally refreshes on every construction, parses and persists accessTokenParsed.data, but then constructs the jsforce Connection with accessToken: credentialKey.access_token (the old token from before the refresh) and the old instance_url. The new access token is never used for API calls, so an expired stored token still fails, while every service construction now adds a Salesforce token request and a DB write. It also bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, so it does not honour credential-sync mode.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared non-constant-time and errors are unhandled
findings.body: The shared secret is compared with !== against a request header, which is timing-unsafe for a secret that alone authorizes overwriting any user's third-party credentials for any app. The handler also has no method check and no try/catch around appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) (line 31) or symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse (lines 57-59), so malformed or wrongly-encrypted payloads throw unhandled 500s instead of controlled 400 responses. The secret check should use a constant-time comparison and parsing/decryption failures should be caught.
